techniques.name: Reward Hacking Detection
techniques.description: Reward hacking is when an agent trained to maximise a proxy reward (a score that only approximates what its designers want) raises that score by exploiting its gaps while the intended outcome stalls or worsens. Detection scores each trained policy (the agent's decision rule) on the proxy and on an independent measure of the intended objective that training never used, such as a true reward from a simulator, a held-out 'gold' reward model or human ratings. Repeating this at every saved training checkpoint and model size matters because the originating study found capability thresholds at which the true reward drops sharply while the proxy keeps rising. When the true objective cannot be scored in operation, the study instead flags a policy whose actions diverge too far from those of a trusted policy that people have already verified. The output is a pair of reward curves showing where they part, or an anomaly score for each candidate policy.

example_use_cases.description: A transport authority training a reinforcement-learning ramp-metering controller in a traffic simulator rewards it on mean vehicle speed, but also logs average commute time for all drivers at every checkpoint. Checkpoints where speed keeps improving while commute time worsens (for example by holding merging cars back indefinitely) are rejected before any field trial.

A team fine-tuning a customer-support language model with reinforcement learning from human feedback scores each checkpoint with its training reward model and with a held-out reward model and a sample of human ratings that the training loop never sees, and stops training at the point where the training reward keeps rising but the held-out scores fall.

Before an insulin-dosing agent trained against a simulator reward goes to clinical evaluation, the developers score every candidate policy on a separate true objective, time spent in the safe blood-glucose range, and exclude any policy whose simulator reward is high but whose time in range is lower than that of the clinically reviewed baseline policy.

A public-health modelling unit that replaces a reviewed epidemic-response policy with a larger retrained one compares the new policy's actions with the reviewed policy's across simulated outbreaks. A divergence score above the threshold set on earlier policies with known outcomes sends the new policy to expert review instead of adoption, because its true outcome cannot be scored before deployment.

limitations.description: Everything rests on the independent measure of the intended objective. When that measure is itself a proxy (a gold reward model, or a small sample of human ratings), a policy can exploit it too, and the comparison then only detects divergence between two imperfect measures. Collecting enough human ratings at every checkpoint is expensive, which is why studies substitute a gold reward model.

It detects gaming only along the dimensions the true measure scores. A policy that exploits something the true objective does not capture (a side effect, a safety constraint, a user group not represented in the ratings) passes the check, so a clean result is evidence about the measured objective only.

The trusted-policy detector is weak and inconsistent. In the originating benchmark every baseline detector scored an area under the ROC curve below 60% on at least one task, and no detector was best on all tasks, so a quiet detector is not evidence that hacking is absent.

The trusted-policy detector flags difference, not harm. It needs a policy that people have already verified, and comparable action distributions from both policies, and a candidate that is genuinely better than the trusted policy can diverge from it and be flagged, which makes false alarms likely when the trusted policy is only moderately good.

Because the onset of reward hacking can be abrupt as capability grows, checking a few checkpoints or one model size can miss it. The comparison has to be repeated at every checkpoint and model size that might be deployed, which multiplies evaluation cost, especially when the true measure needs human raters.

resources.title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
resources.abstract: Reward hacking -- where RL agents exploit gaps in misspecified reward functions -- has been widely observed, but not yet systematically studied. To understand how reward hacking arises, we construct four RL environments with misspecified rewards. We investigate reward hacking as a function of agent capabilities: model capacity, action space resolution, observation space noise, and training time. More capable agents often exploit reward misspecifications, achieving higher proxy reward and lower true reward than less capable agents. Moreover, we find instances of phase transitions: capability thresholds at which the agent's behavior qualitatively shifts, leading to a sharp decrease in the true reward. Such phase transitions pose challenges to monitoring the safety of ML systems. To address this, we propose an anomaly detection task for aberrant policies and offer several baseline detectors.

resources.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
resources.abstract: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart’s law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed “gold-standard” reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

techniques.name: Toxicity Detection
techniques.description: Toxicity detection uses automated classifiers and human review to identify harmful, offensive, or dangerous content in model outputs. This technique employs tools trained to detect toxic language, hate speech, threats, and other harmful content through targeted testing with adversarial prompts. Detection covers explicit toxicity (slurs, threats, graphic content) and implicit harm (manipulative advice, dangerous instructions). For bias and fairness evaluation of model outputs, see related techniques such as few-shot fairness evaluation and demographic parity assessment.

example_use_cases.description: Screening a chatbot's responses for toxic language, hate speech, and harmful content before deployment in public-facing applications where vulnerable users including children might interact with it.
Screening an AI writing assistant for educational content to ensure it maintains appropriate language and doesn't generate offensive material that could be harmful in classroom or academic settings.

Screening a mental health support chatbot to ensure it doesn't generate stigmatising language about mental health conditions, substance use, or marginalised communities, which could cause harm to vulnerable patients seeking help.

limitations.description: Toxicity classifiers themselves may have biases, potentially flagging legitimate discussions of sensitive topics or minority language patterns as toxic.
Context-dependent nature of toxicity makes automated detection challenging, as the same phrase may be harmful or harmless depending on usage context.
Evolving language and cultural differences mean toxicity definitions change over time and vary across communities, requiring constant updating.
Sophisticated models may generate subtle bias or coded language that evades automated detection while still being harmful.

Comprehensive toxicity detection often requires human review to validate automated findings and handle edge cases, which is resource-intensive and may not scale to high-volume applications or real-time content generation.

Toxicity classifiers require large labeled datasets of harmful content for training and validation, which are expensive to create, emotionally taxing for annotators, and raise ethical concerns about exposing people to harmful material.

Configuring detection thresholds involves tradeoffs between false positives (over-censoring legitimate content) and false negatives (missing harmful content), with different stakeholders often disagreeing on acceptable balance points.
Detection performance often degrades significantly for non-English languages, code-switching, dialects, and internet slang, limiting effectiveness for global or multilingual applications.

resources.title: RealToxicityPrompts: Evaluating Neural Toxic Degeneration in Language Models
resources.abstract: Pretrained neural language models (LMs) are prone to generating racist, sexist, or otherwise toxic language which hinders their safe deployment.We investigate the extent to which pretrained LMs can be prompted to generate toxic language, and the effectiveness of controllable text generation algorithms at preventing such toxic degeneration.We create and release RE-ALTOXICITYPROMPTS, a dataset of 100K naturally occurring, sentence-level prompts derived from a large corpus of English web text, paired with toxicity scores from a widelyused toxicity classifier.Using REALTOXICI-TYPROMPTS, we find that pretrained LMs can degenerate into toxic text even from seemingly innocuous prompts.We empirically assess several controllable generation methods, and find that while data-or compute-intensive methods (e.g., adaptive pretraining on non-toxic data) are more effective at steering away from toxicity than simpler solutions (e.g., banning "bad" words), no current method is failsafe against neural toxic degeneration.To pinpoint the potential cause of such persistent toxic degeneration, we analyze two web text corpora used to pretrain several LMs (including GPT-2; Radford et al., 2019), and find a significant amount of offensive, factually unreliable, and otherwise toxic content.Our work provides a test bed for evaluating toxic generations by LMs and stresses the need for better data selection processes for pretraining.

resources.title: A New Generation of Perspective API: Efficient Multilingual Character-level Transformers
resources.abstract: On the world wide web, toxic content detectors are a crucial line of defense against potentially hateful and offensive messages. As such, building highly effective classifiers that enable a safer internet is an important research area. Moreover, the web is a highly multilingual, cross-cultural community that develops its own lingo over time. As such, it is crucial to develop models that are effective across a diverse range of languages, usages, and styles. In this paper, we present the fundamentals behind the next version of the Perspective API from Google Jigsaw. At the heart of the approach is a single multilingual token-free Charformer model that is applicable across a range of languages, domains, and tasks. We demonstrate that by forgoing static vocabularies, we gain flexibility across a variety of settings. We additionally outline the techniques employed to make such a byte-level model efficient and feasible for productionization. Through extensive experiments on multilingual toxic comment classification benchmarks derived from real API traffic and evaluation on an array of code-switching, covert toxicity, emoji-based hate, human-readable obfuscation, distribution shift, and bias evaluation settings, we show that our proposed approach outperforms strong baselines. Finally, we present our findings from deploying this system in production.

A Human-centered Evaluation of a Toxicity Detection API: Testing Transferability and Unpacking Latent Attributes
resources.abstract: Perspective is a publicly available, machine learning API that can score text for toxicity. It is available for use in online platforms and communities to limit toxicity and promote civil dialogue. In this work, we adopt a human-centered approach to evaluating Perspective by investigating if human ratings of toxicity align with Perspective’s toxicity scores. We also test its transferability by making this comparison for comments from three platforms that have different commenting styles and moderation strategies: news websites, YouTube, and Twitter. Apart from toxicity, the main attribute, we collect participant ratings for three additional attributes: respectfulness, formality, and presence of stereotypes. While disrespect is part of how Perspective defines toxicity, formality and presence of stereotypes were included in the study to explore if they could be hidden/latent attributes that affect toxicity scores from Perspective. We analyzed how participant ratings for these additional attributes vary with respect to Perspective’s toxicity score for comments from each platform. We find that for high toxicity scores, Perspective strongly aligns with participant ratings of toxicity and disrespectfulness across all three platforms, providing weak evidence of its transferability. However, our evaluation also surfaced formality and presence of stereotypes as latent attributes that are unrecognized parts of Perspective’s scores. We discuss how and why this evaluation is “human-centered,” the importance of conducting such evaluations, and implications of these results for content moderation in social platforms.

resources.title: An Evaluation of the Google Perspective API by Race and Gender
resources.abstract: Research on American politicians demonstrates that minority politicians often face higher rates of uncivil speech online.While previous studies have focused on federal representatives, local politicians engage more frequently with constituents, increasing the risk of online and offline violence.These imminent threats to state-level officials highlight the need for tools that can measure the toxic discourse faced by local politicians, making algorithmic evaluation of these tools essential for understanding these interactions.To this end, this study evaluates the Google Perspective API, a widely used machine learning algorithm that quantifies toxicity.This study assesses the performance of the API across various demographic identities.Using a dataset of one million tweets directed at state legislators across all 50 states in January 2021, I identify significant gender and racial discrepancies in the algorithm's performance.Specifically, the API demonstrates better performance in predicting toxicity toward men than toward women.The racial discrepancies are slightly more nuanced with the API performing better for some races and not others.This research underscores the importance of algorithmic validation and has implications for studies of algorithmic performance, online harassment and political communication.

techniques.name: Scenario-Based Simulation Testing
techniques.description: Scenario-based simulation testing checks an automated system, most often an automated driving system, by running it through a planned set of situations in a simulator and judging each run against criteria fixed in advance. Scenarios are written at three levels of detail: a functional scenario describes a situation in words (a car cuts in ahead on a motorway), a logical scenario turns it into parameters with ranges (speeds, gaps, road friction), and a concrete scenario fixes one value for every parameter so that the run can be reproduced exactly. Functional scenarios are derived from hazard analysis and from the operational design domain (the conditions the system is designed to work in), and concrete scenarios are sampled from the logical ranges, either to cover the whole range or to seek out rare, critical combinations, or are reconstructed from recorded incidents. Each concrete scenario is executed with the system under test in the loop, and pass or fail is decided against its expected behaviour, such as no collision, or by criticality measures such as time-to-collision, giving a record of which situations the system handles and which it does not. ISO 34502 gives a scenario-based safety evaluation framework of this kind for automated driving systems on limited-access highways.

example_use_cases.description: A developer of a motorway driving function derives cut-in, cut-out and stopped-vehicle scenarios from its hazard analysis, gives each logical scenario ranges for speeds, gaps and road friction, and runs several thousand sampled concrete scenarios in simulation for every software release, holding back any release in which a run ends in a collision the function was required to avoid.

A robotaxi operator rebuilds the fatal crashes recorded over a decade in the city where it operates as concrete simulation scenarios, and replays each one with its driving system in place of first one human driver and then the other, so that it can show regulators how the system behaves in the crash types that actually occur in its operating area.

An operator of an autonomous passenger ferry tests its collision-avoidance planner on head-on, crossing and overtaking encounters described in the international collision regulations, varying the other vessel's speed, bearing and visibility in a ship simulator, and checks in every run that the ferry keeps its required passing distance and makes the manoeuvre the regulations call for.

limitations.description: The evidence covers only the scenarios that were specified. Real operating conditions cannot be listed exhaustively, so a clean result shows that the system handles the catalogue, not that it is safe; the safety argument depends on how completely the functional scenarios were derived from the hazard analysis and operational design domain, which needs independent review.

Results are only as credible as the simulation. If the models of sensors, vehicle dynamics or other road users have not been validated against the real world, a system can pass in simulation and fail in operation, so key scenarios should be repeated on a test track or against recorded real data.

How concrete scenarios are sampled shapes what the results mean. Covering whole parameter ranges ignores how often each situation occurs, and searching for critical corner cases finds failures efficiently but over-represents rare situations, so neither supports a statement about real-world accident rates unless results are weighted by how often scenarios occur.

Pass criteria encode a judgement about acceptable behaviour. 'No collision' misses near misses and lucky escapes, while criticality measures such as time-to-collision need thresholds that the developer must choose and justify, and the verdicts change with them.

Building scenario catalogues, simulation environments and behaviour models for other road users takes specialist effort and substantial computing. ISO 34502 applies only to limited-access highways, so for urban roads, ships and other domains the scenario structure, pass criteria and coverage argument have to be built without the standard's support.

resources.title: Scenarios for Development, Test and Validation of Automated Vehicles
resources.abstract: The latest version of the ISO 26262 standard from 2016 represents the state of the art for a safety-guided development of safety-critical electric/electronic vehicle systems. These vehicle systems include advanced driver assistance systems and vehicle guidance systems. The development process proposed in the ISO 26262 standard is based upon multiple V-models, and defines activities and work products for each process step. In many of these process steps, scenario based approaches can be applied to achieve the defined work products for the development of automated driving functions. To accomplish the work products of different process steps, scenarios have to focus on various aspects like a human understandable notation or a description via state variables. This leads to contradictory requirements regarding the level of detail and way of notation for the representation of scenarios. In this paper, the authors discuss requirements for the representation of scenarios in different process steps defined by the ISO 26262 standard, propose a consistent terminology based on prior publications for the identified levels of abstraction, and demonstrate how scenarios can be systematically evolved along the phases of the development process outlined in the ISO 26262 standard.

Waymo simulated driving behavior in reconstructed fatal crashes within an autonomous vehicle operating domain
resources.abstract: Preventing and mitigating high severity collisions is one of the main opportunities for Automated Driving Systems (ADS) to improve road safety. This study evaluated the Waymo Driver's performance within real-world fatal collision scenarios that occurred in a specific operational design domain (ODD). To address the rare nature of high-severity collisions, this paper describes the addition of novel techniques to established safety impact assessment methodologies. A census of fatal, human-involved collisions was examined for years 2008 through 2017 for Chandler, AZ, which overlaps the current geographic ODD of the Waymo One fully automated ride-hailing service. Crash reconstructions were performed on all available fatal collisions that involved a passenger vehicle as one of the first collision partners and an available map in this ODD to determine the pre-impact kinematics of the vehicles involved in the original crashes. The final dataset consisted of a total of 72 crashes and 91 vehicle actors (52 initiators and 39 responders) for simulations. Next, a novel counterfactual "what-if'' simulation method was developed to synthetically replace human-driven crash participants one at a time with the Waymo Driver. This study focused on the Waymo Driver's performance when replacing one of the first two collision partners. The results of these simulations showed that the Waymo Driver was successful in avoiding all collisions when replacing the crash initiator, that is, the road user who made the initial, unexpected maneuver leading to a collision. Replacing the driver reacting (the responder) to the actions of the crash initiator with the Waymo Driver resulted in an estimated 82% of simulations where a collision was prevented and an additional 10% of simulations where the collision severity was mitigated (reduction in crash-level serious injury risk). The remaining 8% of simulations with the Waymo Driver in the responder role had a similar outcome to the original collision. All of these "unchanged" collisions involved both the original vehicle and the Waymo Driver being struck in the rear in a front-to-rear configuration. These results demonstrate the potential of fully automated driving systems to improve traffic safety compared to the performance of the humans originally involved in the collisions. The findings also highlight the major importance of driving behaviors that prevent entering a conflict situation (e.g. maintaining safe time gaps and not surprising other road users). However, methodological challenges in performing single instance counterfactual simulations based solely on police report data and uncertainty in ADS performance may result in variable performance, requiring additional analysis and supplemental methodologies. This study's methods provide insights on rare, severe events that would otherwise only be experienced after operating in extreme real-world driving distances (many billions of driving miles).

In simulated reconstructions of the fatal crashes recorded in its operating area, the driving system avoided every crash in which it replaced the driver who initiated the conflict, and the crashes it did not avoid when replacing the responding driver are reported with their causes.
The ferry's collision-avoidance planner kept the required passing distance in every simulated head-on, crossing and overtaking encounter across the specified ranges of speed, bearing and visibility.
The scenario catalogue used for release testing covers every hazardous event identified in the hazard analysis and the full operational design domain, as confirmed by independent review.

techniques.name: Malicious Model-File Scanning
techniques.description: Malicious model-file scanning checks a downloaded or received model file for code that would run when the file is loaded, without loading it. Several common ways of saving (serialising) models can carry such code, above all Python's pickle format, the default for PyTorch checkpoints and the usual format for scikit-learn models, whose files can instruct the loader to import and call any Python function, so that loading an untrusted file can hand an attacker control of the machine; since version 2.6 PyTorch's own loader by default allows only a small set of known-safe functions, but some libraries switch that off to load their models. The named method is ModelScan, an open-source scanner from Protect AI, which chooses a check by file extension and reads the file as data: for pickle-based files it lists the functions the file would import and compares them with a graded list of unsafe ones, such as the os, subprocess and socket modules and Python's built-in eval and exec, and for Keras and TensorFlow files it flags Lambda layers, which hold arbitrary Python, and operations that read or write files. It reports each finding with a severity from critical to low and exits with a non-zero code when it finds any, so a pipeline can stop the file before anything loads it. The evidence is a record that no listed unsafe call was found in the files scanned; unlike data-poisoning detection it examines the saved file rather than the training data, and it shows neither that the file is safe, nor how the model behaves, nor who produced the file.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's machine-learning platform team adds a ModelScan step to the job that imports models from public hubs into its internal registry. A critical or high-severity finding stops the import and opens a ticket for the security team, which decides whether the third-party checkpoint may enter the registry at all.

A university's research-computing service scans every checkpoint users upload to shared GPU storage, including PyTorch .pt files and scikit-learn models saved with joblib, before jobs on nodes shared between research groups can load them, and quarantines any file with a critical finding until its owner explains the flagged imports.

A manufacturer's operational-technology security team scans each Keras visual-inspection model delivered by an outside contractor before it is copied to factory edge devices. A flagged Lambda layer is accepted only after the contractor supplies the layer's source code and an engineer confirms that it does nothing beyond resizing and normalising images.

limitations.description: It finds only what is on its list. In a peer-reviewed comparison ModelScan missed 9 of 84 known malicious models: five called functions not on its list (the authors' own example wrote files through Python's pathlib module instead of open), three loaded a further payload at run time, for example through numpy.load, and one hid its payload after an early stop instruction, where the scanner stopped reading. A clean scan shows that no known pattern was found, not that the file is safe.

Attackers adapt faster than the list. A peer-reviewed study (2026) found 22 routes by which five frameworks load pickled data, 19 of which evaded all four scanners it tested, ModelScan included, and in a 2026 preprint ModelScan detected none of 3,000 new attack files. A scan is only as current as the scanner release and unsafe list it ran with.

It checks only the files and formats it recognises, chosen by file extension, and skips the rest, so a pass can cover only some of what the loader will open. Showing that a model was checked needs the list of skipped files (ModelScan can print it) and a check that every file the loading code reads was among those scanned.

Findings need judgement. Every Keras Lambda layer is flagged, though Lambda layers are meant for ordinary pre- and post-processing, and benign models from some libraries import functions that pickle scanners treat as suspicious (one peer-reviewed study describes a widely downloaded model flagged this way). Someone able to read the flagged imports or layer code, or to question the model's author, has to decide each case.

It looks for code that runs on load, not for harmful behaviour in the weights. A model whose weights were altered to carry a backdoor, or that was trained on poisoned data, contains no unsafe call and scans clean, as does any file in a format that cannot hold code, such as safetensors; ModelScan's own documentation notes that weights can be manipulated in such formats. techniques.name: AutoAttack
techniques.description: AutoAttack is a fixed suite of four automated adversarial attacks, introduced by Croce and Hein (ICML 2020), that measures how much of an image classifier's test accuracy survives small, deliberately chosen changes to its input images at inference time. The evaluator states the threat model, a norm and radius that bound the change (for example, no pixel value changed by more than 8/255 under the L-infinity norm), and the standard version then attacks each correctly classified test image in turn with APGD-CE (projected gradient descent that sets its own step size, on the cross-entropy loss), a targeted APGD on the authors' Difference of Logits Ratio loss, a targeted form of the FAB minimum-norm attack, and the Square Attack, which needs only the model's outputs and so still works when gradients are uninformative. An image counts as robust only if none of the four finds a misclassified version within the bound, and because every attack setting is fixed in advance the evaluator tunes nothing, which removes a common cause of overstated robustness: an attack too weakly tuned for the model. The output is robust accuracy, the share of test images still classified correctly under attack at the stated norm and radius, reported beside clean accuracy; published models are compared on the RobustBench leaderboard, which uses AutoAttack as its standard evaluation. Because AutoAttack is not built around any one defence, it can supply the attack step for a wider judgement of a defence, such as whether adversarial training holds up against attacks it was not trained on; unlike red teaming, it involves no human attacker or open-ended search.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model-risk team validating a vendor's classifier that recognises which of 40 identity-document types a customer has photographed during remote account opening, so the right authenticity checks run, receives the model weights under the review agreement. It reruns the vendor's robustness evaluation with standard AutoAttack at the same L-infinity radius, compares the two robust accuracies and records any automatic warnings before accepting the vendor's figure.

A photo-sharing platform's trust-and-safety team expects uploaders to perturb images to slip past the classifier that sorts uploads into a dozen prohibited-content categories and an allowed class. Choosing between two candidate models, it runs standard AutoAttack on both at a perturbation budget agreed with its security team, and selects the one with higher robust accuracy whose clean-accuracy cost is acceptable, recording both figures in the release review.

A research group proposing a new defence for a traffic-sign classifier runs standard AutoAttack before publication and finds that the Square Attack lowers robust accuracy further than the gradient-based attacks, one of AutoAttack's warning signs that gradients are masked. It treats its figure as an upper bound and has an attack designed for its defence built before claiming any robustness.

A computational-pathology group comparing a convolutional network and a vision transformer for three-way tumour subtyping on routine slide images attacks both with AutoAttack, its settings reduced for three classes, at several perturbation sizes below what a blinded clinical reader could detect, and compares attack success rates on an external patient cohort to decide which architecture goes forward.

limitations.description: Robust accuracy from AutoAttack is an upper bound: an image counts as robust because these four attacks failed, not because no adversarial example exists. The authors present it as the minimum test for a new defence rather than the strongest possible attack, so a claim that no change within the bound can alter a decision needs a certified-robustness method instead.

The standard version can overstate robustness for defences that are randomised, not differentiable or run an optimisation loop at inference. The reference code warns about some of these cases, offers a version averaging gradients over the model's randomness, and recommends attacks built for the specific defence; RobustBench excludes such defences. A defence tuned to beat AutoAttack itself can pass it without being robust.

The result holds only for the norm and radius tested. It gives no direct evidence about patches, rotations, physical changes to objects or natural corruptions: in RobustBench's quick-start guide, L-infinity-robust models do much worse than an undefended model on fog-corrupted images, though better on average across corruption types. Benchmark radii such as 8/255 are conventions, so the radius should be justified from the deployment's threat, and a new norm or radius needs a new run.

It needs white-box access: three of the four attacks use the model's gradients, and the code expects raw scores (logits) and inputs scaled to [0, 1]; with access only to output scores, the Square Attack can run alone, a weaker test. The standard settings also assume ten or more classes, since the targeted attacks each try nine other classes; on a binary or few-class model the reference code stops with an error, so the settings must be reduced and the result is no longer the standard one.

The full evaluation is computationally heavy for large models and test sets: each white-box run uses 100 iterations, the targeted attacks each try nine target classes, and the Square Attack makes up to 5,000 queries per image. RobustBench's quick start runs a cheaper two-attack version on 50 images and notes the full version is slower but more accurate; a figure from a subset should be reported with its sampling error.

resources.title: Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks
resources.abstract: The field of defense strategies against adversarial attacks has significantly grown over the last years, but progress is hampered as the evaluation of adversarial defenses is often insufficient and thus gives a wrong impression of robustness. Many promising defenses could be broken later on, making it difficult to identify the state-of-the-art. Frequent pitfalls in the evaluation are improper tuning of hyperparameters of the attacks, gradient obfuscation or masking. In this paper we first propose two extensions of the PGD-attack overcoming failures due to suboptimal step size and problems of the objective function. We then combine our novel attacks with two complementary existing ones to form a parameter-free, computationally affordable and user-independent ensemble of attacks to test adversarial robustness. We apply our ensemble to over 50 models from papers published at recent top machine learning and computer vision venues. In all except one of the cases we achieve lower robust test accuracy than reported in these papers, often by more than $10\%$, identifying several broken defenses.

techniques.name: Canary Exposure Testing
techniques.description: Canary exposure testing measures how strongly a training procedure makes a generative sequence model, such as a language model, memorise rare sequences, by planting random secrets (canaries) in the training data and scoring how much the trained model favours them over values it never saw. Because the secrets are random and their values known, the result is calibrated in a way that tests on real records are not and can be compared across model versions, training settings and numbers of repetitions; unlike extraction or membership inference testing of a finished model, it requires control of the training run, and unlike differential privacy auditing, which also plants records, it gives a memorisation score rather than a statistical bound on epsilon. The tester chooses a format such as 'my account number is' followed by a blank, fills the blank with random values to make several canaries, inserts each into the training data a chosen number of times (for example once, ten times and a hundred times), and trains with the settings used in production. Each canary is then ranked by how probable the trained model finds it compared with every other possible filling of the blank, and its exposure is the base-2 logarithm of the number of possible fillings minus the base-2 logarithm of that rank: about 1 for a canary the model treats like any other value, rising to its maximum when the canary is the model's top choice, the level at which a search over the possible fillings can extract it outright. For large spaces of values the rank is estimated by fitting a distribution to the probabilities of a sample of alternatives, and results are usually plotted as exposure against number of insertions.

example_use_cases.description: An email provider training a reply-suggestion model on users' messages inserts seven-word canaries with random middle words between 1 and 10,000 times each into a training run with the production settings, plots exposure against the number of insertions, and uses the curve to limit how often any rare phrase from a single user may appear in the training data before the model is offered to all users.

A bank's machine learning team choosing among learning-rate schedules and model sizes for an autocomplete model trained on transaction descriptions trains each candidate with the same random account-number canaries at the same insertion counts, and picks the configuration with the lowest exposure among those within a set margin of the best validation accuracy.

A health-records software vendor uses the test as a regression check: each time its clinical-text model is retrained on new notes, the same canaries are inserted at fixed frequencies, and the build fails if the exposure of a canary inserted only once rises above a threshold agreed with the vendor's information governance team.

limitations.description: It needs control of the training run. Canaries must be in the data before training, so the test cannot be applied to a model someone else trained or has already released, and it must use the production settings (optimiser, epochs, model size, hyperparameters), because each of these changes how much is memorised; a test model trained differently says little about the deployed one.

It measures memorisation of the planted secrets, not of the real data. Canaries are random and unlike the rest of the data by design, while real personal data that is repeated, structured or similar to other text can be memorised differently, and the choice of format and of random values changes the result. Low exposure for the canaries does not show that no real record can be extracted.

Exposure is not a privacy guarantee. Its scale depends on the number of possible fillings, so values compare only across canaries with the same number of fillings, and it is not an epsilon: in the original study, models trained with differential privacy at budgets too weak to mean anything (epsilon up to 10^9) still showed negligible exposure, so low exposure cannot stand in for a formal bound.

It needs the model's probability for arbitrary sequences, so a system that returns only its single best output needs a different measure. When the space of possible fillings is too large to score in full, exposure is estimated by fitting a distribution to a sample of alternatives; the estimate depends on that fit holding in the far tail and can exceed the true maximum.

techniques.name: Differential Privacy Auditing
techniques.description: Differential privacy auditing tests whether a training procedure that claims a differential privacy guarantee at a stated budget (epsilon, where smaller means stronger privacy) loses more privacy in practice than the claim allows, by measuring a statistical lower bound on its true epsilon. The guarantee itself comes from a mathematical proof, and membership inference testing reports attack success on real records for any model; the audit instead controls which records are present and asks whether the code that was run honours the proof, so it can expose an implementation bug or accounting error but can never confirm the guarantee. The auditor builds two training sets that differ only by one or a few planted records, called canaries and often crafted to be easy to detect, trains the model many times on each, and applies a fixed test to every trained model to guess whether the canary was present. Confidence intervals for the test's true-positive and false-positive rates, such as Clopper-Pearson intervals for a proportion, are converted into a value of epsilon that the procedure must exceed at a stated confidence level, such as 99 per cent; a bound above the claimed epsilon shows that the claim is false for that implementation. Because hundreds of training runs are costly, a later design needs only one: many canaries are each included or left out at random, the test guesses which were included, and the share of correct guesses gives the bound, which is looser than the many-run design's.

example_use_cases.description: Before an NHS trust releases a readmission-risk model trained with an open-source differential privacy library at a claimed epsilon of 3, its data science team audits the exact code and settings: it trains several hundred models with and without a planted mislabelled record and signs off only if the 99 per cent lower bound stays below 3, recording that the audit could have caught a violation but cannot prove the guarantee.

The maintainers of a differentially private training library run a white-box audit on every release: the auditor sees each intermediate model update and inserts a gradient crafted to be easy to detect, so a change to the clipping or noise-sampling code that silently weakens the guarantee pushes the lower bound above the budget the library reports and fails the build.

A mobile keyboard team training a next-word model with federated learning under a claimed user-level guarantee adds simulated canary users to its single production training run, each included or left out at random and enough of them that a bound above the claim is reachable, and checks the one-run lower bound against the claim, because retraining the federated model hundreds of times is not feasible.

limitations.description: A result below the claim proves nothing. The bound is only as strong as the audit behind it: weak canaries, a test that sees only the final model, or too few runs or canaries can give bounds far below the claimed epsilon (one library's documented single-run audit with 1,000 canaries reported 0.42 for a model trained at epsilon 68.5, and 5.5 for one trained without differential privacy). Only a bound above the claim is conclusive, and a pass must not be reported as confirming the guarantee.

The number of training runs caps what can be detected. With 500 runs per training set and 99 per cent confidence, the largest bound the original method can report is about 4.5 even if the test never errs, so it cannot show a claimed epsilon of 8 to be false; larger budgets need many more runs or a different design. In the single-run design the number of canaries sets the cap in the same way.

Bounds come close to the claim only under the strongest access. For DP-SGD on natural data, audits match the claimed epsilon when the auditor sees every intermediate update and inserts crafted gradients, the setting the standard proof assumes. With crafted input records, seeing every update helps only slightly over the final model, and with the final model most of the original audit's bounds were roughly 7 to 12 times below the claim. A result holds only for the access and canaries it assumed.

It is expensive. The original method trained 500 models per training set to choose the test's threshold and another 500 per set to estimate its error rates, which is impractical for large models. The single-run design avoids this but gives looser bounds, which weaken further when only the final model is seen and the model cannot memorise all the canaries or other training data is added.

It checks one implementation, configuration and pair of datasets. A change of clipping norm, batch size, random initialisation or library version needs a new audit, and canaries that are typical rather than worst-case can miss a violation that affects only unusual records, giving false confidence about the risk to outliers.

techniques.name: Training Data Extraction Testing
techniques.description: Training data extraction testing measures how much of its training text a generative language model reproduces word for word when it is sampled, without the tester supplying any training record to look for. It differs from membership inference testing, which starts from a candidate record and asks only whether that record was used in training, and from canary exposure testing, which needs secrets planted before training. The tester prompts the model with empty prompts or a few words taken from public text, generates a large volume of output (from tens of millions to billions of tokens) with the sampling settings the deployed system uses, and checks it against the training corpus: any span of at least a fixed length, such as 50 tokens, found verbatim in an index of the corpus, and not low-entropy filler such as repeated characters or lists of numbers, counts as extracted, and personal data is checked by tagging names and identifiers in the output and looking them up in the corpus. Where the corpus cannot be searched, the outputs are ranked by how much more probable the model finds them than a smaller reference model or a text-compression algorithm does, and the top-ranked candidates are checked by hand, for example by web search. The result is the share of generated text copied from training data (under the hand-checked route, the number confirmed among the candidates checked), the number of distinct passages extracted, and the passages themselves, each with a count of the training documents that contain it: a passage found in one or two documents is a privacy finding in a way that a licence or news story repeated thousands of times is not.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's privacy engineering team fine-tunes an open-weight language model on ten years of customer-service chat transcripts to draft replies for agents. Before deployment it generates 50 million tokens from public-text prompts with the production sampling settings, searches an index of the transcripts for 50-token matches, and looks up every account number, name and phone number tagged in the output. It runs the same test on the base model as a control.

A hospital research group that trained a clinical note-completion model on de-identified discharge summaries runs the test before sharing the weights with partner hospitals. Besides searching for verbatim passages of the summaries, it tags patient names, dates of birth and NHS numbers in the generated text and looks each up in the training set, to find identifiers the de-identification step missed and decide whether the summaries must be re-scrubbed and the model retrained.

An AI developer preparing an open-weight release compares two checkpoints, one trained on a deduplicated copy of the pre-training corpus. It generates text from each at budgets of 100 million and 1 billion tokens, counts distinct 50-token passages found verbatim in the corpus, and compares how the counts grow with the budget, not a single rate, before choosing which checkpoint to release and what to say about memorisation in the model card.

A government department running a citizen-facing chat assistant on a model it fine-tuned on casework correspondence repeats the test after every fine-tuning update. Because chat-tuned models can leak little under ordinary prompts yet emit training text once pushed off their chat behaviour, the test also uses prompts asking the assistant to repeat a single word many times, a pattern that made one production assistant reproduce its training data.

limitations.description: The result is a lower bound set by the effort spent. The number of distinct passages extracted keeps growing as more text is generated, and one study found that a model which leaked more than another at a small budget leaked less in total. A clean result, or a comparison of models at one fixed budget, can therefore mislead; report the generation budget and compare models at several budgets.

Much memorised text comes out only after the right prompt. In one study, sampling from short public prompts recovered about a third of the passages a model was known to reproduce when given their true opening words, and a chat-tuned model leaked far less under ordinary prompts than when pushed into repeating a word. A low rate under ordinary prompts is weak evidence that the data cannot be extracted.

The verdict depends on what the output is checked against and on the match rule. A public proxy for an unavailable corpus undercounts (in one study a 9 TB proxy found under half the matches a manual web search found), and a minimum match length long enough to rule out coincidence misses short secrets such as phone or account numbers unless they are tagged and looked up separately. Paraphrased leaks and facts stitched together from several documents are not counted.

It is costly at a useful scale. One study generated a billion tokens per model, and its whole evaluation, including a 45 TB index built over a 9 TB corpus, took three weeks on a large cloud machine. The test also produces copies of any personal data the model leaks, which must be stored, reviewed and deleted under the same controls as the training data.

It shows what the model emits, not what an attacker could infer. It does not say whether a known person's record was used in training, and it gives no bound for data the test did not happen to elicit, so a clean result cannot stand in for a formal guarantee such as differential privacy.

techniques.name: Dangerous Capability Evaluation
techniques.description: Dangerous capability evaluation measures whether a frontier AI model can carry out tasks that could enable severe harm, such as finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, persuading or deceiving people, acquiring resources and running copies of itself, or helping to plan an attack with chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear materials, and compares the results with capability thresholds that the developer's safety framework fixes before testing. Evaluators first write a threat model for each risk domain; the framework names a critical capability level, at which the model could pose an extreme risk without extra safeguards, and an early-warning trigger defined on the evaluation results, which the method's originators sketched for one domain as success on more than half of a set of tasks given ten attempts at each. They then build task suites for each domain, such as capture-the-flag hacking challenges in sandboxed networks or multi-step tasks that require the model to set up a cloud server and install software, and try to draw out the model's best performance: it is tested without the safety filters of the deployed product, given agent scaffolding (prompts, planning loops and tools such as a command shell) and sometimes fine-tuned, because the evaluation must not underestimate what the model can do. Scoring records success over repeated attempts and, for tasks the model cannot finish, how close it came, by starting it from intermediate milestones and measuring how much expert help it needs to succeed. Unlike red teaming, which probes a system and its safeguards for whatever failures can be found, and unlike tests of whether a model refuses harmful requests, it measures what the model is able to do, and whether the results cross the trigger informs decisions on deployment and on the security measures the model needs.

example_use_cases.description: A frontier AI developer runs its cyber-offence task suite on each major checkpoint during training and before release, using the agent scaffold its evaluation team has found strongest. Its safety framework sets an early-warning trigger on the share of professional-level capture-the-flag challenges solved; a checkpoint that crosses it cannot be released until stronger protection of the model weights and mitigations against cyber misuse are in place.

A national AI security institute given access to a model before release runs autonomy tasks, such as setting up a cloud server and installing an open-source model on it, both end to end and from intermediate milestones, with a staff member approving each action the agent takes on the live internet. It reports to the developer how close the model came to completing each task and how this compares with the developer's previous model.

A company preparing to publish a model's weights openly evaluates a version fine-tuned on task-relevant data as well as the version it plans to release, because anyone who downloads the weights can fine-tune them, and compares the fine-tuned version's results with its threshold when deciding whether to publish.

limitations.description: A result below the threshold is only as strong as the effort spent drawing out the model's capability. Better scaffolds, more attempts, fine-tuning or a later checkpoint can raise scores, and models can be prompted or fine-tuned to underperform deliberately on dangerous-capability tasks while scoring normally elsewhere, so a negative result is a lower bound on capability, not proof of its absence.

The link between a task score and real-world harm is weakly grounded. The method's originators describe their early-warning trigger as early thinking in an extremely immature area and set no thresholds for their chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear evaluations, where most scientific information is dual-use, so different developers can draw the line in different places and reach different decisions from the same scores.

Task suites cover only the threat models someone has written down, and laboratory tasks may not reflect real conditions: persuasion measured in short dialogues with paid participants, or hacking measured on capture-the-flag challenges, may overstate or understate what the model could do against real people and real systems.

Agentic tasks need sandboxed environments, many repeated runs and expert grading, and tasks with real internet access need a person to approve each action so the agent cannot cause harm, which makes full runs slow and costly. Testing the unfiltered model also needs access that external evaluators may not have; testing the deployed product with its safety filters measures something different.

Results date quickly. Scores change with each new checkpoint and fine-tuning recipe, so evaluations have to be repeated for every significant model update, and published tasks can leak into training data, which is why the originating team withheld solutions and flag values from the tasks it released.

techniques.name: Data Validation Checks
techniques.description: Data validation checks apply a written set of rules about what valid data look like to every new batch of data before a model is trained on it or uses it to make predictions, and flag or hold back any batch that breaks them. In Great Expectations (GX Core), a widely used open-source library for this, each rule is an expectation, a declarative assertion such as that a column exists and has a given type, has no missing values or takes values only from an allowed set or within a range (rules on single values can allow a stated share of rows to fail), or keeps a summary statistic (its mean, a quantile, or the divergence of its histogram from one built on reference data) within bounds the team sets. Expectations are grouped into a suite that a checkpoint runs on each batch as it arrives; the result records for every rule whether it passed and how many values broke it, with examples, configured actions can alert the team or update a human-readable report, and the pipeline can be set to stop training or scoring on a batch that failed. Running the same suite on training batches and on the data a deployed model receives catches differences between the two, such as a feature that is always missing in production, before they degrade predictions; unlike out-of-distribution detectors, the checks need no model and judge whole batches against explicit rules rather than scoring single inputs, and unlike runtime monitoring of a deployed model they act before the model sees the data. Unlike a kernel two-sample test, its distribution rules are fixed bounds set by the team, not a statistical test of whether two samples differ.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider feeds surveillance track reports into a model that predicts aircraft arrival times. Its data engineers run an expectation suite on every incoming batch, covering required fields, units, plausible ranges for altitude and ground speed, and the share of reports with missing positions, so that a sensor change that silently switched altitude from feet to metres would stop the batch before it reached the model rather than surface weeks later as worse predictions.

A weather service that retrains a statistical correction model each month on station observations validates every monthly extract first: station identifiers must come from the station list, temperatures must lie within each station's climatological limits, no variable may have more than 2 per cent missing values, and each variable's mean and quantiles must stay within bounds set from earlier years. A failed check stops the retraining and opens a ticket listing the failing stations.

A hospital running a deterioration-risk model on laboratory results checks each hourly batch from the laboratory system against expectations for test codes, units and value ranges, so that if a laboratory changes the unit of a test without notice the batch is flagged and risk scores for the affected patients are withheld until the mapping is corrected.

A bank's credit-scoring team runs the expectation suite written for its training data on a daily sample of the applications its deployed model scores and compares the results, so that a field the online form has stopped collecting, which the scoring service quietly fills with a default value, shows up as a difference between training and production data rather than as an unexplained drop in approval rates.

limitations.description: Checks catch only what someone thought to write down. A batch can satisfy every rule and still be wrong in a way no rule covers, such as a changed relationship between two columns or a change in how labels were assigned. GX Core does not infer rules from the data, since its automatic profilers were removed in version 1.0, so each rule has to be specified, and for pipelines with thousands of features that effort can put teams off setting up validation at all.

Bounds for distribution rules are hard to set. Statistical tests on large batches fire on differences too small to matter: in Google's data validation paper, a chi-square test between 100 million points and a copy with 0.01 per cent of them redrawn from a wider distribution raised an alert in 7 of 10 trials, while thresholds on divergence measures such as KL divergence are hard for teams to interpret. Bounds are therefore tuned by trial, risking too many alerts or missed shifts.

The rules describe the input data, not the model's performance. A batch that passes can still produce wrong predictions if the relationship between inputs and outcomes has changed (concept drift), and a batch that fails shows that the data changed, not that predictions got worse, so the checks need pairing with monitoring of performance once outcomes arrive.

Alerts help only if someone acts on them, and rules need upkeep as data legitimately change. In Google's deployment across more than 700 pipelines, new columns, unexpected values and missing columns were the commonest anomalies, most pipelines revised their schema, and between 28 and 100 per cent of fired anomalies of each kind were fixed, which the authors attribute partly to operators missing or ignoring alerts.

The checks work on tables: GX Core connects to data frames, SQL databases and data files, so for images, audio, free text or gridded weather fields the team must first compute a table of properties, such as sizes, value ranges or missing tiles, and write rules about those. This catches broken or truncated inputs but not changes in what the content shows.

techniques.name: Metamorphic Testing
techniques.description: Metamorphic testing checks a model or AI system without needing the correct output for each test input, by checking that the outputs for related inputs stand in a relation that must hold if the system works as intended. The tester first writes metamorphic relations from knowledge of the task, each pairing a change to the input with the change it should cause in the output, or with no change: adding fog to a road image should leave a steering prediction within a set tolerance, adding a few stray sensor points outside the road area should not remove any detected obstacle, and rotating a whole flight scenario should leave its outcome unchanged. Existing test inputs (source cases) are transformed into follow-up inputs according to each relation, the system is run on both, and each pair is checked, with numeric outputs often allowed a tolerance. A violation points to a fault or unwanted behaviour without any labelled answer, unless the relation itself is wrong; the output is the violation rate for each relation with the failing pairs, and a relation that holds on every pair shows only that the outputs agree with each other, not that they are right. Prompt robustness testing and causal discrimination testing in this catalogue each apply one family of invariance relations (meaning-preserving changes to a prompt, and a change of protected attribute), and prompt robustness testing also scores the answers against known ones; metamorphic testing is the general procedure for writing and checking any such relation, including relations that say how the output should change, and needs no known answers.

example_use_cases.description: An air navigation service provider evaluating a machine-learning conflict-detection aid for en-route controllers has no ground truth for most replayed traffic samples. Its test team writes three relations: swapping two aircraft's call signs, shifting every timestamp by the same amount, and rotating the whole sample together with its wind field must not change which aircraft pairs are flagged. It runs them on a year of recorded traffic and holds the release until every violation is explained.

A supplier of lidar obstacle perception for driverless shuttles cannot label every frame it records. Following a relation implied by the perception specification, its test team adds a few hundred random points outside the mapped road area to recorded frames and checks that no obstacle detected in the original frame disappears, reporting the share of frames where one does, by number of points added, as a release criterion for each software build.

A weather service testing a neural network that nowcasts rainfall from radar images checks a relation expected from the way rain moves with the wind: away from the domain's edges, shifting the input radar sequence a few grid cells east should shift the forecast rain field by the same amount, within a tolerance set from the model's day-to-day error. Forecasters review the breaking cases to judge whether the model has learnt a dependence on location, such as on terrain, that it should keep.

A bank moving its credit-scoring models to a new library cannot treat every difference from the old library's outputs as a fault, since the solvers differ. Its validation team writes relations the mathematics guarantees: reordering the input columns, or adding a constant to a numeric input in training and scoring data of a logistic regression with an unpenalised intercept, must leave every predicted probability unchanged within solver tolerance. Each violation is investigated as a fault.

limitations.description: Passing shows that outputs are consistent, not that they are correct. A model that gives the same wrong answer for a source case and its follow-up satisfies the relation, and one that is wrong in the same way everywhere can pass every invariance relation. On its own the technique therefore does not suit systems where each output must be shown to be right, and it complements rather than replaces testing against known answers where those exist.

The evidence is only as good as the relations, which are written by hand from domain knowledge, with no systematic way to choose among the many possible ones. A relation the system is not bound to obey produces false alarms: in a study of the Weka library, violations by its nearest-neighbour classifier came from legitimate tie-breaking between equally likely labels, not from faults. An incomplete set of relations gives false confidence.

Most model outputs need a tolerance, and the result depends heavily on it. In the DeepTest study of three driving models, violations under simple image transformations fell from 23,391 when a transformed frame's squared error against the human steering label could be at most the original mean squared error to 330 when it could be five times that, and manual review still found false positives. Counts compare only between runs with the same tolerance, set from what the application can accept.

Follow-up inputs are synthetic and may not occur in practice: rain or fog added to an image, or points scattered into a lidar frame, approximate real conditions without reproducing them. A violation on an unrealistic input may not matter in operation, and a pass covers only the transformations tried, so the evidence is about the tested relations and transformations, not the operating conditions as a whole.

A model whose outputs vary between runs on the same input, through sampling, seeds or GPU arithmetic, breaks relations by chance, so runs must be made repeatable or each case repeated and judged statistically. This bites hardest for relations over the training data, such as Xie et al.'s for classifiers, which need the model retrained for every follow-up case; for models that are costly to train only prediction-time relations are practical, and they test the trained model, not its training.

resources.title: Metamorphic Testing: A New Approach for Generating Next Test Cases
resources.abstract: In software testing, a set of test cases is constructed according to some predefined selection criteria. The software is then examined against these test cases. Three interesting observations have been made on the current artifacts of software testing. Firstly, an error-revealing test case is considered useful while a successful test case which does not reveal software errors is usually not further investigated. Whether these successful test cases still contain useful information for revealing software errors has not been properly studied. Secondly, no matter how extensive the testing has been conducted in the development phase, errors may still exist in the software [5]. These errors, if left undetected, may eventually cause damage to the production system. The study of techniques for uncovering software errors in the production phase is seldom addressed in the literature. Thirdly, as indicated by Weyuker in [6], the availability of test oracles is pragmatically unattainable in most situations. However, the availability of test oracles is generally assumed in conventional software testing techniques. In this paper, we propose a novel test case selection technique that derives new test cases from the successful ones. The selection aims at revealing software errors that are possibly left undetected in successful test cases which may be generated using some existing strategies. As such, the proposed technique augments the effectiveness of existing test selection strategies. The technique also helps uncover software errors in the production phase and can be used in the absence of test oracles.

techniques.name: Explainer Latency Benchmarking
techniques.description: Explainer latency benchmarking measures how long an explanation method takes to produce an explanation for a single prediction, on the hardware, software and settings it will run with, and compares the result with the time that the decision it supports allows. The evaluator first sets the time budget, the share of the time the decision allows that is left for the explanation once the prediction is ready, then runs the explainer exactly as it will be deployed (the same model, background data, number of samples and batch size) on a representative set of real inputs, timing each explanation from request to a result ready to display, after warm-up runs and with one-off set-up costs, such as building the explainer, recorded separately. Because the time varies with the model, the data, the hardware and the load on the system, each configuration is timed many times, as machine-learning inference benchmarks such as MLPerf Inference time a model, under realistic concurrent demand where the explainer runs as a shared service, and the result is reported as a distribution: the median, high percentiles such as the 95th or 99th, the slowest case and the share of explanations over budget. Canha et al.'s benchmark framework for explanation methods, which scores methods on properties measurable without human participants, includes this property under the name speed and rates it on a five-level scale with cut-offs at 0.1, 1, 5 and 10 seconds aligned with human response-time limits; the scale suits comparisons between methods, while a claim about a deployment needs the measured percentiles set against that deployment's own budget. The output is a latency profile for each explainer configuration, recorded with its hardware, software versions and load, which shows whether explanations will arrive in time and lets a team choose between explainers and settings on speed alongside the explanation quality measured by other tests.

example_use_cases.description: A card issuer shows its fraud analysts a feature attribution beside each held transaction and needs it within the two seconds before the review queue refreshes. Benchmarking on the production server at peak queue load, it finds that a sampling-based explainer misses the budget for about one explanation in twenty while an explainer specific to its tree ensemble stays well inside it, and adopts the second once its attributions pass the same faithfulness tests.

A hospital adding an explanation panel to a sepsis-risk alert in its electronic health record agrees with clinicians that the panel must load within one second of a nurse opening the alert. The informatics team times explanations on the hospital's own servers with a week of real alerts at typical volume, reports the 95th percentile and the slowest case against that limit, and repeats the measurement after each model or software update.

An online marketplace shows each seller the main reasons its moderation model held a new listing for review, and the page must update within three seconds. Before launch, the team times the service on its production servers with a week of recorded traffic replayed at its real pace; the first request after each quiet period is far slower because the explainer and its background data load on demand. It keeps a loaded explainer running, re-measures, and reports the slowest case.

limitations.description: Speed and explanation quality trade off through the explainer's settings. Sampling-based explainers run faster with fewer samples or a smaller background dataset, but SHAP's documentation notes that more samples give lower-variance estimates, so a faster setting gives noisier explanations. A latency result holds only for the settings tested, and must be measured at the settings whose faithfulness and stability were checked, or a configuration may meet the budget with untested explanations.

Times depend on the hardware, the implementation and the load at the moment of measurement, which Canha et al. single out as the main caveat on their speed metric, so a figure from a developer's workstation does not carry over to a shared production server or an edge device. Any change to the model, the explainer version, the hardware or the traffic pattern calls for re-measurement, and the configuration must be recorded with the result for it to be checked or repeated.

Claims about the slowest cases need many timed explanations. MLPerf Inference, which sets tail-latency bounds for model inference in the same way, sizes its runs so that a 99th-percentile bound holds with 99 per cent confidence, which at its chosen margin takes about 263,000 queries. A few hundred timings can support a claim about the median but not about the 99th percentile, and a single timed run supports neither.

A fast explanation is not necessarily a good one. Latency says nothing about whether an explanation reflects what the model did or whether people can use it, and it leaves out the time a person needs to read it. It supports a claim about explanations only alongside tests of faithfulness and stability and, where people act on the explanations, a study of whether they can use them within the time available.

The budget has to come from the decision, not from a generic scale. Canha et al.'s cut-offs reflect general limits on human response time, which may be looser or tighter than a particular workflow allows, and a budget that leaves out the time to run the model, move the data and display the result will be met in the benchmark and missed in use; MLPerf likewise derives its server-scenario latency bounds from the user's overall time target.
