techniques.name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
techniques.description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.

example_use_cases.description: A regional electricity distributor deciding whether to replace its regression model for day-ahead substation demand with a gradient-boosted model evaluates both over the last two years, with an origin each day at the time forecasts are issued, a horizon of the next 48 half-hours and weekly refitting, as planned for operation. It compares error at each lead time and in each season, and switches only after finding the new model better in winter peaks as well as on average.

A national weather service's post-processing team testing a machine-learning correction for station temperature forecasts places origins every day over three years, with lead times of one to ten days, and refits the correction monthly as it would in service. Error by lead time and by month shows whether the correction still helps at the longest lead times and whether its gain in winter holds in all three winters rather than one.

A hospital's operations analysts choosing a model to forecast emergency admissions one to fourteen days ahead for staff rotas compare a seasonal statistical model with a neural network, using weekly origins over two years that include two winter peaks. They report error at the seven-day lead time the rota planners use, and keep the simpler model because the neural network's advantage disappears at that horizon.

limitations.description: Refitting at every origin multiplies training cost by the number of origins: daily origins over two years means more than 700 fits. Machine-learning forecasters are often refitted only now and then and otherwise just fed new data, which Hewamalage et al. describe as common practice; that is cheaper but measures something different, so the refit schedule in the evaluation must match the one planned for deployment or the errors do not describe the deployed system.

The time-ordered split prevents leakage only through the split itself. Scaling, smoothing, decomposition, feature selection or tuning done on the whole series before splitting, or features summarising a period not yet over at the forecast time, still let future information in. Hewamalage et al. show a model beating the best possible forecast of a random walk only because a decomposition was fitted to the whole series; every such step must be redone within each origin.

Errors from neighbouring origins share most of their training data and, for multi-step horizons, overlapping test periods, so they are correlated: an average over hundreds of origins is less precise than the count suggests, and the spread across origins is not a confidence interval. Deciding whether one model beats another needs a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors, such as the Diebold-Mariano test, not a plain comparison of average errors.

The first origins have little training data, so their errors can overstate those of a model trained on the full history, and a short series leaves few test periods and a noisy average. For purely autoregressive models (past values as the only inputs) on stationary series, whose errors show no remaining autocorrelation, Bergmeir et al. show that standard k-fold cross-validation remains valid, and Hewamalage et al. recommend it for short series as it uses the data more efficiently.

It measures how the model would have performed over the history available, not how it will perform after a change that history does not contain, such as a new tariff, a replaced sensor or an abrupt structural break; Hewamalage et al. note that no evaluation design can anticipate a break that lies only in the future. Results should be stated for the periods and conditions they cover and repeated as new data arrive.

techniques.name: Deletion and Insertion Curves
techniques.description: Deletion and insertion curves test whether a feature-attribution explanation, such as a heatmap over an image or highlighted words in a text, puts first the input features the model actually relies on. For the deletion curve, the evaluator removes features in the order the explanation ranks them, most important first, replacing each with a neutral value such as zero, the dataset mean, random noise or a blurred copy, and records the model's score for the explained class after each step; a faithful ranking makes the score fall quickly, so a smaller area under the curve is better (equivalently, a larger area over it, the AOPC score Samek et al. report). The insertion curve runs the other way: it starts from an input with every feature removed or blurred, restores features in ranked order, and rewards a fast rise. For text, the same procedure is often reported as comprehensiveness (how far the predicted-class probability drops when the top-ranked words are deleted) and sufficiency (how far it drops when only those words are kept), either at one cut-off or averaged over cut-offs from the top 1% to the top 50% of words. Explanation methods are compared on the same model, inputs and replacement value, against a random ranking as a baseline, and the result shows how well the ranking tracks the model's behaviour, not whether the highlighted features make sense to a person.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's cardiology informatics team has a deep network that measures intervals and amplitudes from 12-lead ECGs and must choose which heatmap method to show cardiologists. It perturbs the highest-ranked sample points first, one per step, tracks the rise in measurement error over several thousand ECGs, and compares each method's area under the error curve with that of random heatmaps. Because expert preferences and the curves can disagree, it reports both before choosing.

A regulator's data team routes consumer complaints with a fine-tuned transformer classifier and wants to highlight for caseworkers the words behind each routing decision. Before choosing between two word-attribution methods, it computes comprehensiveness and sufficiency on a validation sample at the 1, 5, 10, 20 and 50% cut-offs and adopts a method only if it clearly beats randomly ranked words on both measures.

A rail operator's engineering team uses an image classifier to flag defects in track inspection photographs and wants heatmaps that point inspectors to the defect. It runs deletion with pixels set to a constant and insertion from a blurred image for three heatmap methods, then repeats the deletion run with a second replacement value, and adopts a method only if it ranks first under both.

limitations.description: Removing pixels or words produces inputs unlike anything the model was trained on, so part of the drop in score can be the model reacting to an unfamiliar input rather than to the loss of the information the explanation pointed to, and the shape of the removed region can itself carry class information. Results are least trustworthy when large parts of the input are removed; variants that retrain the model or fill removed pixels from their neighbours reduce the effect.

The score depends on how features are removed and in what order. On one image classifier, the best-ranked method changed when removed pixels were set to the dataset mean instead of random colours, removing the least relevant pixels first ranked the methods roughly in reverse of removing the most relevant first, and rankings varied from image to image. A comparison holds only for the stated replacement value, order, step size and fraction removed, and should be checked under a second replacement.

Only the order of the attribution scores counts, not their size, so explanations with very different magnitudes can receive the same score. Taking absolute values of signed attributions changes the order and hence the result. The curves cannot tell an explanation that ranks the right features but gives them misleading magnitudes from one that gets both right; that needs a measure that uses the attribution values.

The curves show whether the ranking tracks the model, not whether the explanation is useful or correct for the domain: a model that relies on a spurious cue receives a faithful explanation of that cue. In a study of ECG models, ECG experts' choice of the best heatmap method disagreed considerably with the perturbation ranking, so a good curve does not show that experts will find the explanation helpful.

Each curve needs one model evaluation per step, for every input and method compared, so fine-grained curves over large images, long documents or big test sets are expensive. In the original region-perturbation study, two settings over 5,040 images each, with 100 steps repeated ten times because the replacement values were random, took roughly 36 hours on a workstation with 20 hyper-threaded Xeon cores in 2015. Coarser steps cut the cost but make the curve less able to separate methods.

techniques.name: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
techniques.description: Sanity checks for saliency maps are two randomisation tests that show whether an explanation method's output depends on what a neural network has learned, or would look much the same for a network that had learned nothing. In the model parameter randomisation test, the evaluator recomputes explanations for a fixed set of inputs after replacing the trained weights with random ones, either cumulatively from the output layer down towards the input (cascading randomisation) or one layer at a time with the others left trained (independent randomisation). In the data randomisation test, the evaluator trains a copy of the same architecture on the training data with the labels shuffled, until it has memorised them, and compares its explanations with those of the model trained on the true labels. Similarity between original and randomised explanations is measured with rank correlation, with and without absolute values, and with image similarity scores such as the structural similarity index; a method whose maps stay similar fails, because its output cannot reflect the learned weights or the relationship between inputs and labels, as Guided Backpropagation and Guided GradCAM failed in the original study when the upper layers were randomised, while plain gradients and GradCAM passed. Passing is a necessary condition, not proof of a good explanation: it shows a method responds to the model, not that its explanations are faithful or useful.

example_use_cases.description: A radiology AI group considering saliency maps as a guide to where a chest-radiograph model sees a pneumothorax runs cascading randomisation on the trained network, measuring structural similarity between original and randomised maps after each block. It sets aside methods whose maps stay similar, as several common methods did in a published study of this task, unless a deletion test shows they still track the model, and uses the rest only alongside a separately validated localisation model.

An insurer's fraud analytics team shows investigators attribution scores for each claim flagged by a neural-network model. Before rollout it runs independent layer randomisation, one layer at a time, and checks that rank correlation without absolute values falls for every layer, so that the scores investigators see depend on the trained weights throughout the network rather than mostly on the claim's raw feature values.

A wind-farm operator's reliability team uses a one-dimensional convolutional network on gearbox vibration signals and gives maintenance engineers heatmaps over each signal. It runs the data randomisation test by training the same architecture on shuffled fault labels until it fits them, and keeps only heatmap methods whose maps differ clearly between the two networks, since a map that survives shuffled labels cannot show what the network learned about faults.

limitations.description: Passing is easy for an explanation that carries no information. Binder et al. show that attribution maps with no correlation between neighbouring pixels score well in model randomisation tests, and that top-down randomisation tends to preserve the scale of forward-pass activations, so even a good explanation can change only so much. They argue the test should not alone decide whether a method is kept: two methods that score poorly on it beat several gradient methods in occlusion-based tests.

The verdict depends on how similarity is measured. In the original study, rank correlation with absolute values and structural similarity stayed high for some methods after randomisation while rank correlation without absolute values fell to near zero, because randomisation flipped signs but kept the input's outline. There is no agreed pass threshold and libraries set their own defaults, so the measure, absolute-value setting and threshold must be reported with the result.

The similarity measures are sensitive to noise, so a method with noisy maps looks changed by randomisation partly because of its own noise, and its score is overstated. Later work proposes repairs: averaging each explanation over noisy copies of the input before comparing (Smooth MPRT), or comparing how much more complex the explanation becomes after full randomisation (Efficient MPRT); its authors report more reliable results with both.

The model parameter test needs the weights and a layered network, so it cannot be run on a model reached only through an interface. The data randomisation test needs the training data and pipeline and a network able to memorise shuffled labels; the original study trained to over 95% training accuracy, which for a large model costs a full training run.

Most evidence for the tests comes from image classifiers. Passing says nothing about whether the highlighted regions match what matters in the domain: in a chest-radiograph study, every saliency method, including those that passed the randomisation test, localised abnormalities worse than a dedicated detection or segmentation network.

resources.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
resources.abstract:
Saliency methods have emerged as a popular tool to highlight features in an input
deemed relevant for the prediction of a learned model. Several saliency methods
have been proposed, often guided by visual appeal on image data. In this work, we
propose an actionable methodology to evaluate what kinds of explanations a given
method can and cannot provide. We find that reliance, solely, on visual assessment
can be misleading. Through extensive experiments we show that some existing
saliency methods are independent both of the model and of the data generating
process. Consequently, methods that fail the proposed tests are inadequate for
tasks that are sensitive to either data or model, such as, finding outliers in the data,
explaining the relationship between inputs and outputs that the model learned,
and debugging the model. We interpret our findings through an analogy with
edge detection in images, a technique that requires neither training data nor model.
Theory in the case of a linear model and a single-layer convolutional neural network
supports our experimental findings.

Gradient-Based Saliency Maps Are Not Trustworthy Visual Explanations of Automated AI Musculoskeletal Diagnoses
resources.abstract: Saliency maps are popularly used to “explain” decisions made by modern machine learning models, including deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). While the resulting heatmaps purportedly indicate important image features, their “trustworthiness,” i.e., utility and robustness, has not been evaluated for musculoskeletal imaging. The purpose of this study was to systematically evaluate the trustworthiness of saliency maps used in disease diagnosis on upper extremity X-ray images. The underlying DCNNs were trained using the Stanford MURA dataset. We studied four trustworthiness criteria—(1) localization accuracy of abnormalities, (2) repeatability, (3) reproducibility, and (4) sensitivity to underlying DCNN weights—across six different gradient-based saliency methods (Grad-CAM (GCAM), gradient explanation (GRAD), integrated gradients (IG), Smoothgrad (SG), smooth IG (SIG), and XRAI). Ground-truth was defined by the consensus of three fellowship-trained musculoskeletal radiologists who each placed bounding boxes around abnormalities on a holdout saliency test set. Compared to radiologists, all saliency methods showed inferior localization (AUPRCs: 0.438 (SG)–0.590 (XRAI); average radiologist AUPRC: 0.816), repeatability (IoUs: 0.427 (SG)–0.551 (IG); average radiologist IOU: 0.613), and reproducibility (IoUs: 0.250 (SG)–0.502 (XRAI); average radiologist IOU: 0.613) on abnormalities such as fractures, orthopedic hardware insertions, and arthritis. Five methods (GCAM, GRAD, IG, SG, XRAI) passed the sensitivity test. Ultimately, no saliency method met all four trustworthiness criteria; therefore, we recommend caution and rigorous evaluation of saliency maps prior to their clinical use.

techniques.name: Appropriate Reliance Measurement
techniques.description: Appropriate reliance measurement tests whether people who receive an AI system's advice follow it when it is right and keep their own judgement when it is wrong, and whether an explanation, or another aid such as a confidence score, moves them towards that pattern. It uses a two-step decision study on a classification task, the only kind Schemmer et al. define it for: for each task item the participant first decides alone, then sees the AI's advice, with or without the explanation, and makes a final decision, on a set of items with known correct answers drawn so that the AI is wrong on a known share of them. Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree are counted, because when they agree the final decision cannot show which source the person relied on. Schemmer et al. define two rates over these items: relative AI reliance, the share of items with a wrong first decision and correct advice on which the person switched to the advice, and relative self-reliance, the share of items with a correct first decision and wrong advice on which the person kept their own answer. Comparing the two rates between an explanation condition and a control condition shows whether the explanation reduces under-reliance (rejecting correct advice), reduces over-reliance (accepting wrong advice) or merely raises agreement with the AI, which overall accuracy or agreement with the AI does not show on its own.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer considering highlighted claim features as an explanation for its fraud-flagging model runs a two-step study with its claims handlers on 40 past claims, with the model wrong on a quarter of them, comparing handlers who see the flag alone with handlers who also see the highlights. It adopts the highlights only if relative AI reliance rises without relative self-reliance falling, since higher acceptance of all advice, right and wrong, would show deference rather than better judgement.

A conservation charity whose volunteers identify bird species with help from an image classifier measures relative AI reliance and relative self-reliance separately for experienced birders and beginners, and for example-based and written explanations. It chooses which explanation to show each group from the results, because a volunteer's expertise changes how an explanation, especially a wrong one, shifts their reliance on the classifier.

A hospital whose safety case for a sepsis alert relies on ward doctors overriding wrong alerts, and whose workflow has doctors record their own escalation decision before the alert appears, runs a vignette study in that workflow, with and without the alert's explanation panel. Before switching the panel on, it reports relative self-reliance, and the share of wrong-alert cases that ended in a wrong decision, against the oversight requirement in the safety case.

limitations.description: The rates describe behaviour on a task set built to contain many AI errors: Schemmer et al. drew equal numbers of items from each cell of the confusion matrix, which put the AI's accuracy on their 16 items at 50%. The study does not show how people rely on advice when errors are rarer, as they usually are in service, so it supports a claim about the conditions tested, not a direct estimate of over-reliance in deployment.

Only items on which the first decision and the advice disagree enter the two rates, so each rate can rest on a handful of items per person, and items on which the person and the AI are wrong together, the errors that oversight cannot catch, enter neither rate. Plan the sample around the expected number of disagreements, and report beside the rates the share of wrong-advice items that ended in a wrong final decision.

Asking for a decision before the advice is shown is itself an intervention. Guo et al.'s reanalysis of an earlier study found reliance closer to the appropriate level when people decided first than when they saw the AI's advice first, so a two-step study may show better reliance than a deployed system that presents the advice straight away.

The rates judge each decision by whether the advice turned out to be right, not by whether following it was the better bet given what the person could see. Guo et al. argue that this outcome-based definition mixes two failures, wrong beliefs about how often the AI is right and poor use of those beliefs, and treats a close call the same as an obvious one, so a low rate does not say which to fix.

Results depend on who takes part and on how good the explanations are. Morrison et al. found that participants' expertise changed how incorrect explanations affected their reliance, and that example-based explanations misled participants more than written ones, so a result from novices, or from explanations that were always correct, does not carry over to expert users or to explanations that are sometimes wrong.

techniques.name: Forward Simulation Test
techniques.description: A forward simulation test checks whether people who have studied a model's explanations can predict the model's output for inputs they have not seen, so it tests with people the understanding an explanation method is assumed to give, where fidelity checks only compare the explanation with the model by computation. Doshi-Velez and Kim proposed it as a human-grounded evaluation of interpretability: participants are given an explanation and an input and must state what the model will output, whether or not that output is correct. In the controlled design of Hase and Bansal, participants study a set of examples with the model's outputs, predict the outputs for a separate set of test inputs, then study the same examples with explanations added and predict the same test inputs again, and the gain in accuracy is credited to the explanations (a separate group that studies the examples without explanations guards against a practice gain); the test inputs are kept apart from the explained examples so that explanations cannot give the answers away, and are chosen so that the model is right and wrong equally often, so that predicting the true label scores no better than chance. A counterfactual variant, in Hase and Bansal's form, shows an input, the model's output and its explanation, and asks what the model will output for an edited version of that input, with edits chosen so that half change the output. The result is the change in the share of correct predictions, with a confidence interval, for each explanation method or design compared; it is evidence that people can anticipate the model on the kind of input tested, not that they make better decisions with it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's model validation team must choose between feature-attribution bar charts and a short rule list as the explanation shown to credit analysts for a loan-default model. It runs a forward simulation test with 30 credit analysts on past applications, balanced between correct and incorrect model predictions, and adopts the rule list only if its gain over the no-explanation baseline is clearly larger than that of the bar charts; otherwise it treats the two as equal.

An online platform's trust and safety team uses the counterfactual variant to test whether moderators who see which words a toxicity classifier weighted can predict whether it will still flag a comment after one of those words is replaced. A score no better than the baseline tells the team that the highlights do not show how the classifier responds to edits, before it writes moderation guidance that relies on them.

A research team choosing between counterfactual images and saliency heatmaps for a chest X-ray pneumonia classifier shows each group of participants explained example images, then asks them to predict the classifier's decision on 12 other images, three from each cell of its confusion matrix, without explanations. It takes forward to a study with clinicians the explanation whose group predicts best, measured against a group that saw the examples without explanations.

A local authority plans to show caseworkers, who are outside the team that built it, the reasons behind a housing-benefit fraud-risk score. Before releasing the reasons in that form, it runs a forward simulation test with caseworkers on unseen cases, half of them cases the score got wrong, using the reasons exactly as they will appear, and revises them if caseworkers who studied them predict the flag no better than caseworkers who did not.

limitations.description: A pass shows that people can anticipate the model, not that they decide better with it. Buçinca et al. found that results on a task of predicting an AI's decisions did not predict results on the real decision task, and Poursabzi-Sangdeh et al. found that people who could better simulate a simple, clear model did not follow it more when that helped, and in some experiments were less able to correct its large mistakes. A claim about decisions needs a decision study.

The test is easily made trivial. If the explained examples are reused as test items, explanations that show the predicted class or a probability give the answer away, and if the model is mostly right, participants can score well by predicting the true label. Hase and Bansal found earlier studies that reused the same items for explanation and prediction; results from such designs overstate what the explanation conveys.

Effects are often small against the variation between people and items. With 32 trained undergraduates and about 180 to 320 responses per condition, Hase and Bansal's 95% confidence intervals on the change in accuracy were about 8 to 13 percentage points either side, and only LIME on tabular data clearly improved both forward and counterfactual simulation. A study must be sized for the difference it needs to detect, with a bootstrap over both participants and items.

The score holds for the people tested. Many studies use students or crowd workers because domain experts are costly to recruit, which Doshi-Velez and Kim give as the reason this kind of evaluation is cheaper; a result from lay participants does not show that the clinicians, analysts or caseworkers who will use the explanation can predict the model.

The before-and-after design credits any gain to the explanations, but participants see the same examples and test items twice, and Hase and Bansal had no group that repeated both phases without explanations, so a practice gain is not ruled out. Their participants also found it hard to remember the explained examples while predicting, so the number of examples and the time allowed must be fixed and reported when methods are compared.

resources.title: Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
resources.abstract: As machine learning systems become ubiquitous, there has been a surge of interest in interpretable machine learning: systems that provide explanation for their outputs. These explanations are often used to qualitatively assess other criteria such as safety or non-discrimination. However, despite the interest in interpretability, there is very little consensus on what interpretable machine learning is and how it should be measured. In this position paper, we first define interpretability and describe when interpretability is needed (and when it is not). Next, we suggest a taxonomy for rigorous evaluation and expose open questions towards a more rigorous science of interpretable machine learning.

techniques.name: Think-Aloud Study of Explanation Use
techniques.description: A think-aloud study of explanation use asks a small number of participants to say what they are thinking while they use an AI system's explanations to do a realistic task, so that the design team can see how the explanation is read, used, ignored or misread. It applies the think-aloud method from cognitive psychology, which rests on Ericsson and Simon's account of verbal reports: people can voice what they are attending to as they work without changing their thinking, provided they are not asked to report things they would not otherwise attend to, such as the reasons for their actions. In a session, a facilitator gives a short practice task, then sets tasks in which the participant sees the model's output and explanation and makes a decision, and while the participant works gives only neutral reminders, such as 'what are you thinking?', when they fall silent; audio and screen are recorded. The recordings are transcribed and coded, often by thematic analysis, into findings such as parts of the explanation that were misread, parts never looked at and questions it left unanswered, and the team changes the design and tests it again. The output is qualitative, design-stage evidence about how an explanation is understood: it can show that a misreading occurs, but not how often it occurs among users or whether their decisions improve.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a nurse-facing explanation for a patient deterioration score runs think-aloud sessions with six ward nurses on a clickable prototype using past patient records. It finds that nurses read a factor that lowered the score as a sign that the patient was improving, relabels the chart, and re-tests the new labels in a second round before fixing the design for a quantitative evaluation.

The developer of a vocal emotion-recognition app that highlights which parts of a recording drove each prediction runs remote think-aloud sessions with a dozen users. One participant reads the highlight colour bar as a trace of the speaker's tone of voice, a misreading that no rating of the explanation would have revealed, and the team changes how the highlight is drawn.

A bank's model risk team preparing to give loan officers counterfactual explanations (for example, the income at which a refused application would have been approved) runs think-aloud sessions with five officers on past applications, including some the model got wrong. It learns which suggestions officers would pass on to applicants and which they reject as implausible, and decides whether to filter the suggestions before release.

limitations.description: How participants are asked to talk changes what is observed. A meta-analysis of 94 studies by Fox, Ericsson and Best found that plain thinking aloud left accuracy unchanged, but that asking people to explain or describe their thinking changed performance, and that verbal reports of every kind tended to make tasks take longer. Facilitators must avoid 'why' prompts, and task times from these sessions cannot serve as performance measures.

Talking through a task can make people attend to an explanation more than they would at work. In Buçinca et al.'s think-aloud study, participants' preferences between two explanation types matched the results of a proxy task rather than those of the realistic task, and the authors suggest thinking aloud pushed people into analytical thinking, so these sessions may overstate how closely users read explanations in normal use.

Studies use few participants (between 4 and 14 in the sources for this record), so a finding shows that a problem exists, not how common it is, and cannot support a claim about the share of users who understand an explanation or about decision quality. The sessions also show only the situations their tasks include: tasks need some wrong model outputs if the team wants to see how people use an explanation when the model errs.

Not everything people do with an explanation gets said. Quick, perceptual uses leave little trace: in Zhang and Lim's study, participants called the audio examples intuitive but did not say why they found them simple. People also tend to say what they think the right answer is, the social desirability bias the GOV.UK guidance warns of. Silence about part of an explanation does not mean it went unused or was understood, and a screen recording or gaze data is needed to tell these apart.

Findings depend on the analyst: coding transcripts into themes is interpretive, so a study meant to support an assurance claim needs a stated coding scheme and a second coder. The voice and screen recordings are personal data that need participants' consent and controlled storage, and recordings made on real cases may also hold personal data about the people those cases concern.

techniques.name: Disaggregated Evaluation
techniques.description: Disaggregated evaluation assesses and reports a system's performance separately for each group of people a claim covers, and for combinations of groups (intersectional groups, such as darker-skinned women), so that a good overall score cannot hide a group for whom the system works badly. Following Barocas et al. (2021), the evaluator first fixes the design choices that change what the evaluation can show: which groups and combinations to report; how other factors that affect performance, such as lighting or recording conditions, are handled (held constant, varied deliberately, or left as they occur); which metrics to use, for a classifier often false positive and false negative rates reported separately, because each can harm different people; and whether the evaluation is exploratory, or confirmatory, meaning that it tests hypotheses stated in advance on data built to hold enough cases in every group. Each metric is then computed on a labelled evaluation set for every group and combination, together with the number of cases behind it and an interval showing how far the estimate could move through sampling alone, obtained for example by resampling the evaluation set. Groups are compared by absolute and by relative gaps, which can tell different stories: false negative rates of 1 and 10 per cent differ by nine points but tenfold. The output is a table or chart of per-group and per-combination results with their case counts and intervals, and a record of the design choices needed to interpret them; it is this design, more than any one metric or interval method, that decides which comparisons the evaluation can support and how conclusive each is.

example_use_cases.description: Before a hospital trust adopts a supplier's skin-lesion classifier, its clinical safety team reports sensitivity and specificity on locally labelled images for each skin-tone group, sex and age band, and for skin tone crossed with sex. Cells holding fewer melanoma cases than the evaluation protocol requires are marked as too small to estimate rather than reported, and the trust collects more images for them before deciding whether the tool may be used for all patients.

A consumer organisation evaluating the speech-to-text services behind automated phone lines has speakers from several regional and ethnic groups, matched on age and gender, read identical scripted passages, and reports word error rate per group with intervals. Because everyone says the same words, a gap can be attributed to how each service recognises speech rather than to what was said, the evidence the organisation needs for a complaint to the providers.

A bank's model risk team runs a confirmatory evaluation of its fraud model each quarter. The groups (age band, sex and their combinations), the metrics (false positive rate, which drives blocked legitimate payments, and false negative rate), the sample and the largest acceptable gap are fixed in a protocol before the data are drawn, and the model stays in service only if every interval for a gap lies inside that margin.

An exam board piloting an automated essay-scoring model runs an exploratory evaluation of its agreement with human markers, split by first language, school type and their combinations. It finds one weak cell, candidates with English as an additional language at small schools, too small to be conclusive, and commissions a confirmatory study with a sample built to fill that cell before deciding whether the scores can count towards grades.

limitations.description: Each attribute added multiplies the number of cells and shrinks each one, so combinations of attributes soon hold too few cases for a stable estimate, and where a cell holds only a few errors, intervals from resampling come out too narrow. Comparing many cells also throws up some large gaps by chance. A confirmatory claim needs enough cases in every cell, which Barocas et al. note existing datasets rarely provide, so the data available limit which comparisons can be tested.

A gap between groups shows that performance differs, not why. Another factor that affects performance may differ between the groups, as with the time between paired images that NIST suggested could explain a higher false negative rate for Asian people in face recognition. Holding such a factor constant hides gaps at its other values, varying it needs the factor labelled for every case, and strongly correlated factors are hard to separate, or impossible when they always occur together.

The result is only as good as two sets of labels. Where ground-truth outcomes are wrong, or recorded differently for different groups, and the extent of the error cannot be identified, Barocas et al. note the results are meaningless however careful the design. Group membership is often ascribed by an institution or inferred from appearance, adding errors and possible harm to those labelled, and datasets may hold few of some groups (darker-skinned women were 4.4 per cent of one benchmark).

It measures differences in performance and nothing else. Equal error rates say nothing about whether outputs stereotype or demean people, or whether favourable decisions are shared in proportion, and narrowing a gap under one metric can open a gap under another. A clean result supports a claim about the performance gaps measured, for the groups and conditions tested, and no wider fairness claim.

Results on a laboratory dataset may not carry over to the system in use, where lighting, recording conditions and operators' decisions differ, and Barocas et al. note that a component's performance alone may say little about the whole system around it. Evaluating in the setting of use captures this but is costly, and is often impossible for an outside evaluator, who usually sees the system only as a black box.

resources.abstract: Recent studies demonstrate that machine learning algorithms can discriminate based on classes like race and gender. In this work, we present an approach to evaluate bias present in automated facial analysis algorithms and datasets with respect to phenotypic subgroups. Using the dermatologist  approved Fitzpatrick Skin Type classification system, we characterize the gender and skin type distribution of two facial analysis benchmarks, IJB-A and Adience. We find that these datasets are overwhelmingly composed of lighter-skinned subjects (79.6% for IJB-A and 86.2% for Adience) and introduce a new facial analysis dataset which is balanced by gender and skin type. We evaluate 3 commercial gender classification systems using our dataset and show that darker-skinned females are the most misclassified group (with error rates of up to 34.7%). The maximum error rate for lighter-skinned males is 0.8%. The substantial disparities in the accuracy of classifying darker females, lighter females, darker males, and lighter males in gender classification systems require urgent attention if commercial companies are to build genuinely fair, transparent and accountable facial analysis algorithms.

techniques.name: Bias Benchmark for Question Answering
techniques.description: The Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) is a fixed set of about 58,500 multiple-choice reading questions that tests whether a language model's answers rely on social stereotypes, across nine social dimensions (age, disability status, gender identity, nationality, physical appearance, race and ethnicity, religion, socio-economic status and sexual orientation) and two combinations of them, using stereotypes documented as harmful in US English-speaking contexts (Parrish et al., 2022). Each item describes two people from different groups and asks a question that points at a stereotype, such as who is bad at maths, with three answers to choose from: either person, or an answer such as 'cannot be determined'; in the ambiguous version the passage does not say which person the question is about, so 'cannot be determined' is correct, and in the disambiguated version an added sentence settles it. Items come in balanced sets that swap the two groups and their order and pair each negative question with a non-negative one, so that a model which simply prefers one group whatever the question is not counted as stereotyping. From the model's chosen answers (generated, or picked by comparing the probabilities it gives the three options) the test reports accuracy in each version and a bias score per category from -100% to 100%: the share of answers naming a person that follow the stereotype, rescaled so that 0 means no consistent direction and a negative score leans against the stereotype, and in the ambiguous version multiplied by the error rate, so that stereotyped guesses weigh more when the model guesses often; it also reports how far accuracy falls when the correct answer goes against the stereotype. Unlike substituting identity terms into a deployer's own inputs, or varying the people shown in few-shot examples, BBQ is a fixed external question set that tests what a model concludes about people when the text does, and does not, support a conclusion.

example_use_cases.description: A government department choosing between three language models for a service that answers citizens' questions about benefits runs the full BBQ set on each, with the same prompt, answer extraction and scoring for all three. It compares accuracy and both bias scores category by category, rules out any model whose ambiguous-context bias score in any category is further from zero, in either direction, than a limit set before testing, and records that the result covers US stereotypes only.

A recruitment software company fine-tuning an open-weight model to answer HR helpdesk questions runs BBQ on the base model and on every fine-tuned version through the same evaluation harness, logging each answer. A release is blocked if any category's ambiguous-context bias score moves further from zero than the base model's by more than an agreed margin, or if the accuracy gap between items whose correct answer matches the stereotype and items whose correct answer goes against it widens.

An NHS trust's digital team preparing a health-information assistant needs evidence about UK stereotypes, which BBQ was not built for. Following the procedure used to build a Korean version, it keeps templates that transfer, changes target groups where UK stereotypes differ, drops those that do not apply, writes UK-specific ones, surveys members of the UK public to confirm each stereotype and its target group, and reports results on the original and adapted sets side by side.

limitations.description: BBQ's stereotypes, and most of its categories, come from US English-speaking contexts, and its authors say results should not be used as evidence about other cultures. Adapting it to Korean meant changing target groups, dropping templates and adding four categories, and a machine-translated BBQ gave different bias scores from the adapted version (Jin et al., 2024). For a UK deployment the original set says nothing about UK-specific stereotypes.

A low bias score is weak evidence that a model is unbiased. Each category rests on about 25 templates with very short passages and three fixed answers; the authors warn that a low score is not proof of an unbiased model, and that for a model used on very different text BBQ is unlikely to be a valid measure. It counts only stereotypes that change the chosen answer, so it misses bias that shifts the model's probabilities without changing its choice.

The bias score leaves out 'cannot be determined' answers and has a sign, so it must be read with accuracy and by its distance from zero. A model that always gives that answer has full accuracy and a zero bias score on ambiguous items, yet fails every disambiguated one. A negative score means answers lean against the stereotype, as HELM found for most of the models it tested (Liang et al., 2023); a one-sided limit such as 'below 5%' passes such a model.

Scores depend on the prompt format and on how answers are extracted or scored, so they compare only across models tested the same way. In the original study one UnifiedQA model, given the same items in two input formats, scored 2.4 and 18.6 on ambiguous gender-identity items. Results for a single template rest on few items (one reported example has 72), so they are noisy and should be combined across templates for the same stereotype.

It is weak evidence about bias against people with two combined identities. In the original study, results on the two intersectional categories (race by gender, race by socio-economic status) were too inconsistent for the authors to conclude that models responded to more than one aspect of identity, and the lm-evaluation-harness task notes that these categories are not really taken into account in its bias scores.

Holistic Evaluation of Language Models
resources.abstract: Language models (LMs) are becoming the foundation for almost all major language technologies, but their capabilities, limitations, and risks are not well understood. We present Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) to improve the transparency of language models. First, we taxonomize the vast space of potential scenarios (i.e. use cases) and metrics (i.e. desiderata) that are of interest for LMs. Then we select a broad subset based on coverage and feasibility, noting what's missing or underrepresented (e.g. question answering for neglected English dialects, metrics for trustworthiness). Second, we adopt a multi-metric approach: We measure 7 metrics (accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency) for each of 16 core scenarios when possible (87.5% of the time). This ensures metrics beyond accuracy don't fall to the wayside, and that trade-offs are clearly exposed. We also perform 7 targeted evaluations, based on 26 targeted scenarios, to analyze specific aspects (e.g. reasoning, disinformation). Third, we conduct a large-scale evaluation of 30 prominent language models (spanning open, limited-access, and closed models) on all 42 scenarios, 21 of which were not previously used in mainstream LM evaluation. Prior to HELM, models on average were evaluated on just 17.9% of the core HELM scenarios, with some prominent models not sharing a single scenario in common. We improve this to 96.0%: now all 30 models have been densely benchmarked on the same core scenarios and metrics under standardized conditions. Our evaluation surfaces 25 top-level findings. For full transparency, we release all raw model prompts and completions publicly for further analysis, as well as a general modular toolkit. We intend for HELM to be a living benchmark for the community, continuously updated with new scenarios, metrics, and models.

techniques.name: Rich Subgroup Fairness Auditing
techniques.description: Rich subgroup fairness auditing checks whether a binary classifier treats any subgroup much better or much worse than the population as a whole, where the subgroups are not a short list chosen in advance but every group that rules of a chosen kind over several protected attributes can describe, such as everyone for whom a weighted sum of age, sex and ethnicity indicators exceeds a threshold. Kearns, Neel, Roth and Wu (2018) proposed it to detect what they call fairness gerrymandering: a classifier can have equal false positive rates for men and for women, and for each ethnic group, yet very unequal rates for particular combinations, such as women of one ethnicity. For a chosen rate (the false positive or false negative rate, or in the paper also the rate of positive decisions), each subgroup is scored by the gap between its rate and the overall rate multiplied by the share of all records that are in the subgroup and count towards that rate (for the false positive rate, those with a negative true outcome), so a gap counts for more the larger the group, and the audit searches for the subgroup with the highest score. Exact search is computationally hard in the worst case, so it is posed as a weighted (cost-sensitive) classification problem over the protected attributes and solved approximately: the reference implementation fits two linear regressions that propose a candidate worst subgroup as a linear threshold rule, using only those attributes, the true outcomes and the classifier's decisions, not the model itself. The output is that rule with the subgroup's size, rate and weighted gap (called gamma), compared with a limit set beforehand; unlike reporting metrics for groups listed in advance, the audit finds subgroups nobody listed, and unlike multiaccuracy boosting, which checks a score's average error in each subgroup and then corrects the model, it compares a decision rate with the overall rate and changes nothing.

example_use_cases.description: A lender's model risk team validating a credit-risk model before release audits its decisions on a held-out sample of past applicants whose repayment is known, and records that these are only applicants the old policy approved. It searches subgroups over age, sex, ethnicity and disability status for the worst false positive rate gap (good payers flagged as high risk), compares it with a limit agreed with the risk committee, and sends the rule for any subgroup over it to the developers.

A hospital's clinical AI team has confirmed that a sepsis early-warning model misses cases at similar rates for men and women and for each recorded ethnic group. Before rollout it audits the false negative rate over subgroups combining age, sex and ethnicity and, because the search is approximate, also scores a grid of rules over two of the attributes by brute force, as the method's authors did, to check the search did not miss a larger gap.

A local authority's internal audit team re-audits a model that flags housing benefit claims for fraud review each quarter, using a random sample of claims reviewed whether or not they were flagged. It records the worst subgroup by false positive rate (legitimate claims flagged) over age, sex, ethnicity and disability, with its size and gap, and escalates to the system owner when the weighted gap exceeds the agreed limit.

limitations.description: Finding the worst subgroup exactly is hard in the worst case, even for conjunctions or linear thresholds of attributes (Kearns et al. 2018, Theorem 3.3), so practical audits use a heuristic search. A subgroup it reports does have the measured gap on the audit data, but a clean result is only a lower bound: the authors note their auditor could miss a larger disparity and checked it by brute force on two attributes (Kearns et al. 2019). 'Nothing found' is a search result, not a proof.

Gaps are weighted by subgroup size, which the authors require for reliable estimates and which lets small groups pass with large gaps: a subgroup holding 2% of the records whose false positive rate is 20 percentage points above the overall rate scores at most 0.004, under the 0.005 limit used in the AIF360 demonstration. The audit cannot support a claim about a small named group; report that group's own rate, with an interval, instead.

Only subgroups that the rule class can describe, over the attributes designated as protected, are searched; the reference implementation uses linear threshold rules. The class has to be limited because, as the authors note, any imperfect classifier could be accused of unfairness to the set of people it misclassifies. A protected attribute that is not recorded or not designated is invisible, so the attributes used and their encoding must be stated with the finding.

Error-rate audits need the protected attributes and the true outcome for every audited record, which a deployed system may not supply, for example when outcomes are seen only for approved applications. Reliable estimates need more data the richer the subgroup class, the authors' experiments report in-sample results, and the tools give no confidence interval, so audit on held-out data and repeat on fresh data before relying on a worst-case figure.

It tests parity of one rate at a time for binary decisions, each subgroup's rate against the overall rate. A pass on false positives says nothing about false negatives, the AIF360 auditor implements only those two error rates, and other criteria, such as whether scores mean the same in every subgroup (calibration), need a different test. The rate must be chosen to match the fairness claim before the audit.

resources.title: Preventing Fairness Gerrymandering: Auditing and Learning for Subgroup Fairness
resources.abstract: The most prevalent notions of fairness in machine learning fix a small collection of pre-defined groups (such as race or gender), and then ask for approximate parity of some statistic of the classifier (such as false positive rate) across these groups. Constraints of this form are susceptible to fairness gerrymandering, in which a classifier is fair on each individual group, but badly violates the fairness constraint on structured subgroups, such as certain combinations of protected attribute values. We thus consider fairness across exponentially or infinitely many subgroups, defined by a structured class of functions over the protected attributes. We first prove that the problem of auditing subgroup fairness for both equality of false positive rates and statistical parity is computationally equivalent to the problem of weak agnostic learning — which means it is hard in the worst case, even for simple structured subclasses. However, it also suggests that common heuristics for learning can be applied to successfully solve the auditing problem in practice. We then derive an algorithm that provably converges in a polynomial number of steps to the best subgroup-fair distribution over classifiers, given access to an oracle which can solve the agnostic learning problem. The algorithm is based on a formulation of subgroup fairness as a zero-sum game between a Learner (the primal player) and an Auditor (the dual player). We implement a variant of this algorithm using heuristic oracles, and show that we can effectively both audit and learn fair classifiers on a real dataset.

techniques.name: Actionable Recourse Audit
techniques.description: An actionable recourse audit checks whether the people a linear classifier refuses, for example for a loan, a job interview or a public service, could change that decision through actions open to them, and how much they would have to change. The auditor first writes an action set saying which features can change and how: immutable features such as age stay fixed, features such as education level can only rise, and each changeable feature gets bounds and a grid of realistic values. Then, for each refused person in a sample drawn from the population the model will serve, an integer programming solver (optimisation software that searches discrete choices exactly) looks through the permitted actions for the cheapest change that flips the decision, measuring cost as the largest shift, in population percentiles, that the change makes to any one feature, and either returns that action or proves that none exists, which a search that simply fails to find a counterfactual cannot do. The audit reports the share of refused people who have recourse and the distribution of its cost, which can be compared across candidate models or broken down by group, and the same solver can list a refused person's cheapest alternative changes (a 'flipset') for a decision notice. Unlike the Contrastive Explanation Method, which explains one prediction through features that must be present or absent, or Diverse Counterfactual Explanations (DiCE), which searches any model for several alternative inputs that would change one decision, the audit works only on linear models but certifies whether any permitted action exists and summarises the answer across a population.

example_use_cases.description: Before launching a linear model that ranks applications to a housing support scheme, a local authority's analytics team audits recourse on last year's applicants, with age and household size fixed. Its report to the scheme's oversight board gives the share of refused applicants who could qualify through changes the scheme expects, such as completing a tenancy course, and how large those changes are, so the board can decide whether to approve the model.

A credit card issuer generates a flipset for each applicant its linear scorecard declines and puts the two cheapest items in the decline letter, for example reducing current debt to a stated amount, together with the other scored features the applicant should keep unchanged, so that following the stated actions would change the decision under the current model.

A lender's model risk committee is shown recourse audits for candidate credit models of almost equal accuracy. It rejects the most accurate, under which some refused applicants had no feasible action because of an 'ever defaulted' feature, adopts a variant that uses recent defaults only, and has the audit re-run each quarter on new applicants, watching younger applicants, who were scarce in the training data.

An employer's analytics team audits its linear screening model for interview invitations and compares the cost of recourse for refused women and men with similar predicted scores. Sex is not a model input, but the cost can still differ by sex. Refused candidates' true suitability is never observed, so the team cannot also match on outcome as the originating study did, and reports any gap with that caveat to its fairness review panel, which decides whether the features need revising.

limitations.description: The proof that no action exists depends on the model being linear, such as logistic regression, a linear support vector machine or a rule set that can be written in linear form. For tree ensembles or neural networks, a local linear approximation can still suggest actions, which then have to be checked on the real model, but a failure to find one proves nothing, so the share of refused people without recourse is no longer a certified figure.

Every conclusion rests on the action set and cost the auditor chooses. Bounds that are too tight make people appear to lack recourse; loose bounds let a model 'provide' recourse only through drastic changes, which shows only as high cost; and the default cost treats a one-percentile change as equally hard in every feature unless someone who knows the domain sets how much harder some changes are.

The search treats features as changing independently unless the auditor adds constraints. Real actions have knock-on effects: raising income can also raise savings, so a listed action may cost more than needed, or may not change the decision once its effects on other features are counted, as Karimi, Schölkopf and Valera showed for recourse methods that ignore causal relations between features.

Recourse is defined for a fixed model. After retraining, an action given in an earlier notice may no longer change the decision, so the audit has to be re-run after each update. An action that changes the prediction need not change the real outcome either: showing a refused applicant how to be approved can lead them into credit they cannot repay.

A flipset lists only the features to change, so a person who also changes an undisclosed feature may still be refused unless the notice says what must stay the same. The originating paper builds flipsets from public credit datasets and does not test whether refused people understand them or can act on them. Owners may also resist publishing flipsets, because many of them together can let others reconstruct the model.
